q: A patient with moderate COPD needs an arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. Which block gives good analgesia with the lowest risk of hemidiaphragmatic paresis?
o: Combined suprascapular and axillary nerve blocks
why: Interscalene blocks cause phrenic nerve block in nearly all patients, which may be poorly tolerated with respiratory disease. Suprascapular nerve block (supplying most of the shoulder joint) plus axillary nerve block, or a superior trunk block with low volumes, provides useful analgesia with much less diaphragmatic impairment. Infraclavicular and axillary blocks do not reliably cover the shoulder.

q: At which level of the brachial plexus does the supraclavicular approach deposit local anaesthetic?
why: Interscalene: roots/trunks (C5–C7, often sparing C8–T1 and the ulnar nerve). Supraclavicular: trunks and divisions, where the plexus is compact, giving dense block of the whole arm ('spinal of the arm'). Infraclavicular: cords around the axillary artery. Axillary: terminal branches (musculocutaneous often needs a separate injection).

q: An 88-year-old with a hip fracture has pain 8/10 despite paracetamol and IV morphine. What is the most appropriate next step according to NICE CG124 and the AAGBI hip fracture guideline?
o: Increase morphine until pain is controlled
Fascia iliaca compartment block (or femoral nerve block)
Wait for spinal anaesthesia in theatre
why: NICE recommends paracetamol and opioids, and adding a nerve block (fascia iliaca or femoral) if analgesia is inadequate; NSAIDs are not recommended in older patients. The supra-inguinal fascia iliaca approach reaches the femoral, lateral cutaneous and sometimes obturator nerves. Pericapsular (PENG) block is an alternative. Blocks reduce opioid use and delirium.

q: For an ankle block for forefoot surgery, which nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve?
why: Four of the five nerves in an ankle block are branches of the sciatic nerve (tibial, deep and superficial peroneal, sural). The saphenous nerve is the terminal branch of the femoral nerve and supplies the medial ankle and foot. The tibial nerve supplies the sole and is the most important for forefoot surgery; block it first because it is the largest and slowest to take effect.

q: In a transversus abdominis plane block, between which two layers is local anaesthetic injected?
o: Rectus abdominis and posterior rectus sheath
why: The TAP lies between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, where the anterior rami of T6–L1 run. TAP blocks give somatic analgesia of the anterolateral abdominal wall (no visceral analgesia). Lateral approaches cover roughly T10–L1 (lower abdomen); subcostal approaches cover upper abdominal dermatomes. Rectus sheath blocks suit midline incisions.

q: Shortly after an axillary block with 30 mL of 0.5% levobupivacaine, a 60 kg patient becomes agitated, then has a seizure and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. According to the AAGBI guideline, what is the initial lipid emulsion dose?
o: Propofol 2 mg/kg in place of lipid
20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 minute, then infusion at 15 mL/kg/h
Lipid only if cardiac arrest occurs
why: AAGBI (2010, endorsed by RA-UK): 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute, then 15 mL/kg/h; repeat the bolus up to twice at 5-minute intervals and double the infusion rate if instability persists; maximum cumulative 12 mL/kg. Treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, support the airway, and continue CPR for prolonged periods if arrest occurs; amiodarone is preferred to lidocaine for arrhythmias. Propofol is not a substitute.

q: A patient has persistent numbness and weakness in the hand a week after an interscalene block. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate MRI of the cervical spine in all cases
Reassure; most resolve so no follow-up is needed
Repeat the block to treat the neuropathy
Document, examine, inform the patient, arrange neurological follow-up and consider nerve conduction studies at about 3 weeks
why: Most post-block neurological symptoms are transient (resolving within weeks to months), and permanent injury is rare. Persistent deficits need examination, documentation, honest discussion, and referral to a neurologist. Nerve conduction studies and EMG are most informative after about 3 weeks and can show pre-existing pathology. Urgent imaging is needed for progressive deficits or suspected haematoma.

q: Which ultrasound probe and frequency is best for a superficial interscalene block?
o: Any probe; frequency does not affect image quality
why: Higher frequencies give better axial resolution but penetrate less (attenuation rises with frequency). Superficial structures (brachial plexus, vessels for cannulation) are best imaged with a high-frequency linear probe. Deep structures (sciatic in large patients, neuraxial, abdominal) need lower-frequency curvilinear probes. Phased-array probes are used for echocardiography.

q: A 20-year-old has a closed tibial shaft fracture fixed with an intramedullary nail. Which analgesic plan best reflects the 2021 consensus on regional anaesthesia and compartment syndrome?
o: Opioids only, with no monitoring needed
Dense continuous popliteal block with 0.5% bupivacaine for 72 hours
Use regional anaesthesia if appropriate, with dilute local anaesthetic, clear communication, and compartment monitoring by a trained team
why: The multidisciplinary consensus (Anaesthesia 2021) found no evidence that regional anaesthesia delays diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome if monitored appropriately. Use lower concentrations and volumes, avoid dense prolonged blocks in high-risk patients, communicate with the surgical team, monitor regularly, and remember that breakthrough pain in a blocked limb is a red flag.

q: Ultrasound before a labour epidural in a woman with a BMI of 48 is most useful for which purpose?
o: Real-time visualisation of the Tuohy needle entering the epidural space
Identifying the midline, the interspace level and the depth to the epidural space
why: Pre-procedural neuraxial ultrasound (paramedian sagittal oblique and transverse views) identifies the midline, interspace and estimated depth to the ligamentum flavum/dura, improving first-pass success when landmarks are difficult. Ultrasound tends to underestimate depth slightly because the probe compresses tissues. Loss of resistance remains the endpoint.

q: For total knee arthroplasty, why is an adductor canal block often preferred to a femoral nerve block?
o: It avoids the need for any other analgesia
It provides better analgesia of the posterior knee
It blocks the obturator nerve completely
It is quicker to perform with nerve stimulation
It largely preserves quadriceps strength, allowing earlier mobilisation
why: The adductor canal contains the saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis (mostly sensory), so quadriceps strength is better preserved than with a femoral nerve block, reducing falls and allowing early mobilisation. It does not cover the posterior knee; IPACK or periarticular infiltration is often added.

q: Which block is one of the RA-UK 'Plan A' blocks every anaesthetist should be able to perform?
why: The seven RA-UK Plan A blocks (2021) are interscalene, axillary brachial plexus, erector spinae plane, rectus sheath, femoral, adductor canal and popliteal sciatic. They were chosen to cover most surgical sites with a manageable set of safe, teachable blocks.

q: What does the 'Stop Before You Block' check aim to prevent?
why: Stop Before You Block is a moment immediately before needle insertion when the anaesthetist and assistant confirm the site and side against the consent form and surgical marking. Wrong-side blocks are a never event.

q: Why can a nerve appear to vanish when the probe is tilted slightly?
why: Anisotropy: the echogenicity of nerves and tendons depends on the angle of the beam, so small tilts change brightness. Optimise with PART (pressure, alignment, rotation, tilt). Shadowing occurs behind bone; enhancement occurs behind fluid-filled structures such as vessels.

q: Which ultrasound control places the narrowest part of the beam at the target depth to improve lateral resolution?
why: Set the depth so the target sits mid-screen, place the focal zone at the target, then adjust gain for overall brightness. Higher frequencies give better resolution but less penetration; deep targets may need a lower-frequency curvilinear probe.

q: On ultrasound, how do arteries and veins typically differ?
why: Arteries are round, pulsatile and resist compression; veins are compressible and may change with respiration. Colour Doppler confirms flow. Checking for vessels along the needle path reduces the risk of intravascular injection.

q: An iPACK block is added to an adductor canal block for knee replacement. What does it target?
o: The saphenous nerve at the ankle
The obturator nerve in the obturator canal
The common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
The femoral nerve in the femoral triangle
why: iPACK (infiltration between popliteal artery and capsule of the knee) blocks posterior articular branches from the sciatic and obturator nerves, improving posterior knee analgesia without foot drop. Adductor canal blocks the saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis, sparing most quadriceps strength.

q: What is the main safety concern after a femoral nerve block for knee surgery?
why: Femoral nerve block causes quadriceps weakness, increasing the risk of falls, which is why adductor canal blocks are preferred for knee arthroplasty. Patients need clear instructions, a knee brace or supervision when mobilising.

q: For foot surgery, a popliteal sciatic block alone leaves which area unblocked?
o: The lateral border of the foot
why: The sciatic nerve supplies the leg below the knee except the medial side, which is supplied by the saphenous nerve (from the femoral). A saphenous block at the adductor canal or below the knee completes the block, and also covers a calf tourniquet better.

q: Which block is most reliable for forearm and hand surgery and carries a risk of pneumothorax?
why: The supraclavicular block targets the compact trunks/divisions ('spinal anaesthesia of the arm') with fast, dense onset, but the pleura lies close beneath, so the needle tip must be seen throughout. It also causes phrenic palsy in up to about half of patients. Axillary blocks avoid both risks.

q: After an interscalene block, a patient develops hoarseness and ptosis. What is the explanation?
why: Common, benign side effects of interscalene block are ipsilateral phrenic palsy (nearly 100%), Horner's syndrome and hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve spread. Serious complications include intrathecal, epidural or vertebral artery injection and nerve injury.

q: For shoulder surgery in a patient with severe COPD, which block gives analgesia with less risk of phrenic nerve palsy than an interscalene block?
why: Diaphragm-sparing alternatives include suprascapular nerve block (± axillary nerve block), a lower-volume or extended interscalene technique, or a superior trunk block. They provide useful analgesia with far less hemidiaphragmatic paresis.

q: During lipid emulsion treatment for LA toxicity, cardiovascular instability persists after the first bolus and infusion. What is the next step?
o: Repeat boluses and double the infusion rate
why: AAGBI: 20% lipid 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute, then 15 mL/kg/h. If unstable after 5 minutes, give up to two further boluses 5 minutes apart and double the rate to 30 mL/kg/h. Do not exceed 12 mL/kg in total. Continue CPR (it may be prolonged) and consider cardiopulmonary bypass.

q: During cardiac arrest from LA toxicity, which drug should be avoided for arrhythmias?
why: Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic and should not be used as an antiarrhythmic in LA toxicity. Also avoid calcium channel and beta-blockers. Amiodarone is suggested; adrenaline doses of 1 µg/kg or less may be preferred.

q: Which factor increases the risk of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
o: Very vascular sites such as intercostal blocks
why: Absorption is highest from intercostal, caudal and epidural sites, then brachial plexus and femoral/sciatic. Risk is increased in the elderly, neonates, pregnancy, cardiac or hepatic disease and with low muscle mass. Ultrasound, adrenaline-containing solutions and incremental injection reduce risk.
